summary: This bash function wraps DuckDB in a Docker container, letting you query CSV/JSON/Parquet files in your current folder from anywhere. It handles setup validation (checking Docker exists and the image is built), manages file permissions (read-only by default unless you pass --write), and runs the container with security constraints while preserving your terminal interaction.

explanations.14: This sets the name of the Docker image we'll use—it's a label that identifies the packaged DuckDB application.
explanations.18: This disables a shellcheck warning because the next line intentionally uses single quotes to prevent the shell from expanding ${HOME} when setting the variable; we want the literal string for display purposes.
explanations.19: We're storing the path as a string that still contains ${HOME} (unexpanded) so when we show error messages to the user, they see the generic form that works for any user, not the expanded home directory of whoever is currently running this.
explanations.21: This checks if the docker command exists in the system by trying to run 'docker' and sending any output to /dev/null; if it fails, we abort with an error.
explanations.26: This checks if the Docker image with our chosen name actually exists on this machine; if it doesn't, Docker will fail later, so we catch it here and give helpful instructions.
explanations.42: We default to read-only mode by setting a suffix that will be added to the volume mount command; this prevents the container from modifying your actual files.
explanations.43: If the first argument is --write, we remove the read-only restriction and use shift to discard that argument so it doesn't get passed to DuckDB itself.
explanations.50: We check if both standard input and standard output are connected to a terminal; if so, we add -t to give DuckDB an interactive terminal, otherwise we omit it to allow piping.
explanations.52: This warns the user that files are read-only, but only when no SQL command was passed (so it's interactive mode) and stdin is a terminal.
explanations.58: docker run starts a new container; --rm automatically deletes it when done, and the flags after it configure networking, filesystem access, and security.
explanations.59: This mounts your current working directory (PWD) into the container at /workspace, with the mount_mode suffix added—either :ro for read-only or empty for read-write.
explanations.62: This creates a temporary filesystem in the container with a 256MB size limit, and forbids executing files or changing ownership within it, limiting what the container can do.
explanations.65: This runs the container as the same user (by ID) who invoked the command, preventing privilege escalation and permission issues with files created inside the container.
explanations.69: In zsh, $? is reserved, so we store the Docker exit code in rc to preserve it before other commands might overwrite it.
explanations.70: If the command failed and files were read-only, we show a tip suggesting the user try again with --write in case the failure was due to write permissions.
